title: Co-Designing a Real-Time Classroom Orchestration Tool to Support Teacher–AI Complementarity
extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to design real-time classroom orchestration support for teachers working in AI-enhanced K–12 classrooms. The central problem is that intelligent tutoring systems and other adaptive learning tools can improve student practice, but they also make it harder for teachers to monitor students, interpret what is happening in real time, and intervene effectively. The authors argue that classroom AI tools should complement, rather than replace, teachers, and that designing such tools requires deep stakeholder co-design and new prototyping methods.

The intervention studied is Lumilo, a wearable mixed-reality tool implemented as smart glasses that surface real-time learning analytics to teachers. Across a series of formative studies, lo-fi and mid-fi prototypes, and replay-based enactments, the researchers worked with middle-school math teachers to identify useful analytics, test display concepts, and refine how information should be presented during live class sessions. The work focused on equation-solving ITS classrooms, especially on what teachers want to see about students’ reasoning, struggle, off-task behavior, misconceptions, and progress.

The study involved middle-school math teachers in multiple schools and districts in the United States, with classroom-based prototyping and piloting in authentic school settings. The main conclusions are that teachers prefer simple, glanceable indicators; want analytics that explain why a signal appears; value access to raw student work alongside automated inferences; and generally want tools that support teacher judgment without taking away autonomy. The paper also concludes that some seemingly attractive automation concepts, such as explicit time-management nudges, may be rejected if they undermine teacher control, and that selective sharing and the ability to override or customize the system are important implementation features.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative/case-study paper using interviews, card sorting, speed dating, prototyping, and classroom piloting, but it is not a controlled efficacy study and reports no causal student-outcome estimates. The evidence is credible for design requirements and implementation insights, but weaker for impact claims.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful benefits for teacher workflow and classroom orchestration, but it does not provide measurable effect sizes on student learning. Impact is therefore promising but unclear from an outcomes-evidence perspective.

interventions.use_case: real-time classroom analytics for middle-school math teachers to detect students’ knowledge, struggle, off-task behavior, misconceptions, and recent progress while students work in an ITS; delivered via wearable mixed-reality smart glasses (Lumilo) and class-level displays to support orchestration decisions

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not report student achievement effects from an intervention trial; instead, it studies how real-time analytics can support middle-school mathematics instruction in ITS classrooms. The relevant mathematical content is equation solving, and the main evidence is qualitative design feedback from 10 teachers in needs-finding studies and 16 teachers in prototyping sessions (plus classroom piloting), showing that teachers wanted support for diagnosing students’ solution paths, misconceptions, and areas of struggle, but were wary of inaccurate or non-actionable inferences.
finding.measure: Qualitative teacher judgments about equation-solving analytics, solution-path visibility, and usefulness of class/student-level mathematical indicators
finding.study_size: n=26 teachers across design studies and prototyping sessions

finding.finding_summary: Teachers strongly valued analytics about student frustration, motivation, and engagement, but also expressed discomfort with automated judgments about motivation such as labeling students as 'careless.' The study therefore suggests potential benefits for timely support of affective and motivational needs, alongside risks of misclassification and stigmatizing inferences.
finding.measure: Qualitative reactions to real-time affect/motivation indicators and concerns about student frustration/carelessness
finding.study_size: n=26 teachers across design studies and prototyping sessions

finding.finding_summary: A central finding is that teachers wanted analytics to improve their real-time metacognitive and decision-making work: prioritizing attention, interpreting why students are stuck, and deciding when to intervene versus hold back. At the same time, they rejected designs that overly automated teacher judgment or undermined autonomy, indicating that the learning benefit depends on preserving teacher agency and actionable interpretation.
finding.measure: Qualitative teacher feedback on decision support, prioritization, diagnosis, and autonomy in classroom orchestration
finding.study_size: n=26 teachers across design studies and prototyping sessions

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s strongest substantive contribution is showing that wearable real-time analytics may reduce teacher orchestration burden by helping teachers monitor many students at once, identify who needs help, and surface actionable class-level patterns without constantly scanning the room. Across formative studies with 10 teachers and prototyping with 16 teachers, participants repeatedly described benefits such as prioritizing help, detecting off-task behavior, and supporting one-to-many attention, while also emphasizing that the interface must avoid distraction and information overload.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported workload, orchestration burden, and perceived usefulness of real-time analytics displays for monitoring and intervention
finding.study_size: n=26 teachers across design studies and prototyping sessions
